basis: Reference class for the landform ratios: the project lead's market evidence bands put Wellington hill land at $800-1200/m2 (midpoint $1000) and Lower Hutt hill land at $400-600/m2 (midpoint $500), and each city's band midpoints are divided by its own hill midpoint so hill is 1.00 by construction.

Wellington flat land $1500-2000/m2 (midpoint $1750) over the Wellington hill midpoint $1000 gives 1.75, Lower Hutt flat land $700-1000/m2 (midpoint $850) over the Lower Hutt hill midpoint $500 gives 1.70, and 1.72 is the adopted average of those two city ratios.

Judgement, set at 1.2 times the flat factor of 1.72 rather than taken from a market band: the earlier value of 3.10 came from the premium flat / sea view band, which describes Seatoun, Oriental Bay and the waterfront and is priced on the view, but elevated flat is now assigned from terrain alone and so picks up every drive-on terrace in Karori, Khandallah, Johnsonville, Maungaraki and Pinehaven, which pricing at 3.10 would badly overvalue - 2.06 pays those a real but modest premium for flat, sunny, easy-to-build-on ground, and leaves the headroom up to about 3.10 to be earned by sea view, winter sun and accessibility multiplying together when those are modelled.

Judgement floor, not a researched figure: no modelled address may be valued below 0.25 of its territorial authority's indexed average land value, which keeps the cheapest hill addresses above an implausible near-zero land value.

Judgement ceiling, not a researched figure: no modelled address may be valued above 4.0 times its territorial authority's indexed average land value, which stops a landform class alone from producing a waterfront-scale outlier.

Judgement, not a fitted coefficient: an address one standard deviation steeper than the rest of its territorial authority and landform class is modelled as worth about 10 percent less than its cohort average, slope entering as the exponent of a multiplicative within-cohort adjustment so that it can only move value between addresses of the same class.

Judgement, not a fitted coefficient: an address standing one standard deviation higher above its surroundings than the rest of its cohort is modelled as worth about 5 percent more - deliberately small, because most of what standing high up is worth is the view and the winter sun, which are priced separately and would otherwise be paid for twice.

Judgement floor, not a researched figure: the terrain modifier may not take an address below 0.70 of its cohort average, which stops one extreme slope value, or a DEM artefact read as one, from modelling a near-worthless section.

Judgement ceiling, not a researched figure: the terrain modifier may not take an address above 1.40 times its cohort average, so that the terrain derivatives on their own cannot manufacture the kind of premium only a view or a waterfront position could justify.

Starting point to be tuned against the observed share of elevated flat land, not a researched threshold: standing 3 m above the mean elevation of the surrounding neighbourhood is roughly what lifts a flat site clear of the water in a 1 percent AEP river or coastal inundation event with a sea level rise allowance on top, which is the physical distinction the elevated flat class is drawn for.

Neighbourhood scale, chosen so that the index measures a terrace against the valley floor it stands above rather than the micro-relief of the section itself: 500 m spans the width of a Wellington gully or a good part of the Hutt Valley floor, while staying local enough that the answer is still about this address. The threshold above is only meaningful against a topographic position measured over this window.

Judgement, not a fitted coefficient: land value is modelled as proportional to the gravity accessibility raised to this power, so it is an elasticity. At 0.5 an address with a quarter of another's accessibility is worth half as much, before the landform and terrain terms. Checked against the spread it gives inside Wellington City: with the 6 km Wellington CBD decay a Tawa address (about 14 km out, gravity about 0.25 against about 0.97 in Thorndon) comes out at about half a Thorndon address, which is the order of the gap between Tawa and Thorndon land rates. Refit against the District Valuation Roll in Phase 5.

Judgement, not a researched figure: an address at a railway station is worth 10 percent more than the same address far from one, decaying with distance (see rail_station_decay_length_m). Sits at the low end of the premiums reported for walkable access to commuter rail, because the Wellington network is dense enough that much of the study area has a station within reach anyway.

Plan value (s2_land_value_implementation_plan.md, Phase 3): the rail premium falls to 1/e of itself 400 m from the station, roughly a five minute walk, so it is about 3.7 percent at 400 m and under 1 percent beyond 1.2 km.

Judgement floor, not a researched figure: the accessibility modifier may not take an address below 0.60 of its cohort average. Wider than the terrain band, because accessibility is the larger within-authority driver -- Wellington City runs from the CBD to Makara -- but still a bound, so that a remote rural address does not collapse to the rate clip on accessibility alone.

Judgement ceiling, not a researched figure: the accessibility modifier may not take an address above 1.60 times its cohort average, so the CBD fringe cannot run away from the rest of its cohort on accessibility alone.

Judgement, not a fitted coefficient: a section's land value is modelled as proportional to its area relative to the territorial authority's assumed lot, raised to this power, so a section twice the assumed lot is worth about 1.41 times as much and half the lot about 0.71 times. Below one because land value grows more slowly than area -- the first few hundred square metres carry the building platform and the access, the rest is garden -- which is why small inner-city sections carry the highest rates per square metre. Set from six hand-checked Wellington City land values on 2026-10-01, which it brings closer without being fitted to them. Refit against the District Valuation Roll in Phase 5.

Judgement floor, not a researched figure: the section size factor is evaluated at no less than 150 m2 of land per rating unit. Below it the curve would be extrapolated far past any section a value is set from -- a 93-unit block on 1,170 m2 is 12.6 m2 a unit, at which a 0.5 elasticity would put its rate at six times its neighbours'. At 150 m2 a unit-titled block's rate is about 1.7 times a 450 m2 section's, in line with central land carrying a premium, and a small freehold townhouse section is treated the same way.

Judgement, not a fitted coefficient: an address's value is multiplied by 1 + this times its sea view share, before it is centred within its territorial authority and landform class. A full 180-degree view across the water (a share of about one half) is worth half as much again as a section with none in the same cohort, which is the gap the elevated flat factor left when it was cut from 3.10 to 2.06 (s2_land_value_implementation_plan.md, Phase 4), and the order of the shortfall in the hand-checked rates of 31 Hay Street, Oriental Bay, and 14 Inglis Street, Seatoun, on 2026-10-01. Refit against the District Valuation Roll in Phase 5.

Judgement floor, not a researched figure: the amenity modifier may not take an address below 0.80 of its cohort average. Having no view is the common case, so the floor only binds on a cohort where nearly every address looks at the sea.

Judgement ceiling, not a researched figure: the amenity modifier may not take an address above 2.00 times its cohort average, so a panorama from a ridge cannot run away from its neighbours on the view alone.

Judgement: the sea view is taken 5 m above the ground at the address, about the eye height on the upper floor or deck of a two-storey house. One height for every address, so a single-storey house is credited with the view from a floor it does not have.

Judgement: rays are cast 5 km, far enough to take in the harbour from the hills around it and short of the far side of Cook Strait, which is a distant glimpse rather than the view a section is priced on.
Setting: rays are cast every 5 degrees, so a view is measured to a share of 1/72 and a gap between two houses narrower than 5 degrees can be missed.

Setting: a DEM cell outside the study area's land polygons counts as sea when it stands no higher than this. The LINZ DEM writes the harbour as elevations either side of zero rather than as nodata; 1 m takes that in and leaves the low land beyond the study area out.

Judgement, not a fitted coefficient: an address at the water's edge is worth 25 percent more than the same address far from the sea, before the view is counted and before it is centred within its territorial authority and landform class. Separate from the view, because closeness to the beach and the water is priced whether or not the sea can be seen from the house -- the front of Lyall Bay or Petone behind a dune or a sea wall. Refit against the District Valuation Roll in Phase 5.

Judgement: the coastal premium falls to 1/e of itself 250 m from the sea, so it is about 9 percent at 250 m and under 2 percent beyond 750 m -- the front few streets of a bay rather than the whole suburb behind it.

Judgement, not a fitted coefficient: a section that gets all the winter sun open ground would is worth 30 percent more than one that gets none, before it is centred within its territorial authority and landform class. Winter sun is what separates a good Wellington section from a bad one -- a gully lot under a ridge to the north against a terrace above the same street -- and what a plain aspect calculation misses (s2_land_value_implementation_plan.md, Phase 4). Refit against the District Valuation Roll in Phase 5.

Setting: the horizon the winter sun is run against is measured 1.5 m above the ground, the garden and the living room rather than the upper floor the view is taken from, because sun on the section is what the land is priced for.
Setting: the first day sampled, 1 June. The window is June and July, the months with the lowest sun and the longest shadows.
Setting: the last day sampled, 31 July.

Setting: the number of days spread evenly across the window. The sun's path changes slowly enough over two months that four days resolve it to well inside the 5-degree ray spacing, and each day sampled adds to the run time.
Setting: the sun is sampled every 15 minutes, so a winter day of about nine and a half hours is about 38 samples and the share is resolved to a few percent.
